sentences.text: The reservoir went down in the drought and the church tower came out of it in the second week of August, and by the Friday there were cars parked all the way along the dam road.
Vera watched it happen from the caravan site with a mixture of feelings she has never entirely sorted out.
The tower was not much to look at.

It was six metres of grey stone with no roof, standing in a plain of cracked mud the colour of a paper bag, and it had a tide mark round it at about the height of a person which was the mark of a normal year.
People walked out to it across the mud, which they were not supposed to do, and stood next to it, and took photographs of themselves next to it, and drove home.
Vera worked at the caravan site in the holidays, cleaning the shower block and handing out the wristbands, and she heard the same four conversations every day for a month.
That it was sad.
That it was fascinating.
That they had seen a programme about one in Spain.

And, from a man on the Thursday who was very pleased with himself, that it was a reminder that nothing lasts, which Vera thought was an odd thing to take from a village that had been deliberately drowned by people who filled in a form.
The newspaper called it *the ghost village*, which Vera's grandmother heard on the radio in the kitchen and responded to with a single syllable.
Her grandmother had been eleven when they flooded it.
That was 1963.

She had been eleven, and had left the house on the twelfth of March with a case and a bird in a cage, and had gone up the hill to the new houses at Aldeia Nova with everybody else, and had never gone back down because there was no back down to go to.
The new houses were fine.
Vera had grown up in one of them.

They had bathrooms and they had been built in a straight line facing the road, and every single one of them was identical, and her grandmother had lived in the same one for sixty-two years and had never once called it anything but *the new houses*.
She was seventy-four now and she lived with them and she had not been out to the dam road all week.
"They're calling it a ghost village," Vera said.
"Mm," said her grandmother.

"Have you been down?" "No." "Are you going to?" Her grandmother put the pan down and looked out of the window at the hill for a moment, and Vera thought she was going to get an answer of some kind, and what she got instead was: "There's four hundred cars on that road and a man selling water out of a van.
No." "It's not, is it." "It's a village," her grandmother said, "with a lot of water on it." She was doing something with beans.
"Ghosts is what you say when you'd rather not say drowned, and drowned is what you say when you'd rather not say we did it on purpose for the electricity."
